title: Indians in China Flag Growing Visa Hurdles and Social Media Restrictions
excerpt: With visa rejection rates approaching 40% and China's Great Firewall blocking everyday apps, the roughly 56,000 Indians living in the country face mounting daily challenges.
body:
• China's new COVA pre-approval visa system has pushed rejection rates for Indian applicants to nearly 40%, with processing times doubling to 45 days or more
  • China's Great Firewall blocks WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook, and Google services, forcing Indians to rely on VPNs that face periodic crackdowns
  • New exit-and-entry regulations published by China's State Council on July 31 add further restrictions, including potential entry bans for false visa statements, effective September 15
  • The challenges persist despite improving India-China diplomatic ties, including the resumption of direct flights and tourist visas in 2025

For the approximately 56,000 Indians living and working in China — students, professionals, entrepreneurs, and families — daily life increasingly involves navigating two parallel systems of restriction: one digital, one bureaucratic.

Members of the Indian diaspora in China have raised concerns over tightening visa processes and the country's pervasive social media censorship, which cuts them off from the platforms they use to stay connected with family and colleagues back home.

A Digital Wall Between Two Worlds

China's Great Firewall, the country's internet censorship apparatus, blocks access to WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook, Google services including Gmail and YouTube, and dozens of other platforms that Indians rely on daily. To access these services, residents must use Virtual Private Networks, which operate in a legal grey area and face periodic crackdowns.

https://x.com/EconomicTimes/status/2083788489842380930

According to VPN monitoring service VPNMentor, China employs deep packet inspection, DNS poisoning, IP blocking, and quality-of-service filtering to restrict access. One 2021 estimate found that China blocked 16% of the top 1,000 global websites.

The impact on Indians in China has been documented for years. When India banned WeChat and other Chinese apps in 2020, Indians living in China found themselves cut off from both sides. Dev Raturi, a Chinese-speaking Indian actor and entrepreneur who has lived in China for over 15 years, told the Global Times at the time that the ban severed his connection with family in India, and Indian friends teaching yoga online were forced to stop working.

"Closing WeChat is a mistake. People are in panic, which will make our life more difficult. WeChat is a very important platform for Indian people who have business interaction with Chinese."

— Imran Brown, Indian tourism practitioner studying in China, to the Global Times

While India's app bans remain in place, Indians in China now face restrictions from both governments — unable to use Chinese apps freely back home or access Indian and global apps while in China without workarounds.

Visa Barriers Multiply

The bureaucratic challenges have grown sharper in 2026. China introduced a new pre-approval system through the China Online Visa Application (COVA) portal in late December 2025, adding a digital vetting stage before applicants can even book an in-person appointment for biometrics.

According to Travel and Tour World, citing industry leaders including Mohak Nahta of visa platform Atlys, this two-stage process has pushed rejection rates to nearly 40%. The pre-approval stage alone takes 10 to 15 days, effectively doubling total processing time. Many applicants receive rejections without explanation, forcing them to restart the process from scratch.

Financial requirements have also tightened. The Chinese embassy now looks for a minimum bank balance of ₹1 lakh (approximately $1,200) maintained consistently over three months — a high bar for students and younger applicants.

Adding to the pressure, China's State Council published new exit-and-entry regulations on July 31, 2026, according to Reuters. The rules, effective September 15, allow Chinese authorities to bar foreign nationals from entering the country for one to five years if they submit false statements on visa applications. The regulations also expand exit bans for Chinese citizens deemed threats to national technology security.

Diplomatic Warmth, Ground-Level Friction

The tightening comes against a backdrop of improving India-China relations at the diplomatic level. Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited China in 2025 for the first time in seven years, meeting President Xi Jinping. Both countries resumed direct flights that year after a five-year hiatus, and India resumed issuing tourist visas to Chinese citizens in July 2025.

India also eased business visa procedures for Chinese professionals in December 2025, dropping additional layers of bureaucratic scrutiny and shortening approval times to under a month, according to Reuters. The move was aimed at addressing production losses estimated at $15 billion over four years in India's electronics sector, according to the Observer Research Foundation.

China reciprocated by issuing over 85,000 visas to Indians in the first quarter of 2025 alone, according to the Chinese Embassy in India.

Yet the ground-level experience for Indians living in China tells a different story. The combination of digital isolation from family and friends through the Great Firewall, tightening visa requirements with high rejection rates, and the constant uncertainty of VPN crackdowns creates a challenging environment for the diaspora community.

What Comes Next

Travel industry experts suggest the current difficulties may represent a "calibration period" as China sets new standards for the post-pandemic era. Ajay Prakash, founder of Nomad Travels, told Travel and Tour World that both travelers and consulates are readjusting after a five-year hiatus in leisure travel.

For Indians currently in China, the advice from immigration consultants is to apply for visa renewals well in advance — at least 45 days before expiry — and to maintain meticulous documentation. On the social media front, securing reliable VPN access before arrival remains essential, as VPN provider websites themselves are often blocked within China.

The disconnect between warming government-level ties and the daily frustrations of ordinary Indians in China highlights a recurring pattern in India-China relations: progress at the summit level does not always translate to smoother experiences on the ground.
image_caption: India's ambassador to China said visa issues remain a top concern as new COVA pre-approval requirements push rejection rates for Indian applicants close to 40 percent.
nri_angle: Indians living in China face a dual squeeze — blocked from global social media by the Great Firewall and confronting rising visa rejection rates — creating daily challenges despite warming diplomatic ties.
